name: Cameroon
card_headline: Biya, 93, has not named the vice president created in April, legislative polls are set for February 2027, and jihadist and separatist violence continues.
card_summary: Paul Biya, 93, won an eighth term in October 2025 with 53.66 percent, a result the runner-up Issa Tchiroma Bakary rejects from exile in The Gambia. Rights groups say at least 48 people were killed in the protests that followed. A vice presidency created in April is still unfilled, and Biya spent about ten weeks in Geneva this summer. Legislative and local elections are set for 7 February 2027. About 2.9 million people need aid. [1][2][3][4][5]
card_local: Journal du Cameroun reports that Biya's own party spokesman called the president's son a credible vice-presidential candidate but said nothing is decided, and The Guardian Post and Cameroon Concord carry the Tchiroma story. [6][7][8]
card_international: Reuters reported Biya reshuffled the military leadership while out of public view for 58 days, and Al Jazeera and AFP report the new February 2027 election date and the Wum school attack. [9][4][10]
card_scholar: Carnegie's Lesley Anne Warner says an empty vice presidency would leave an untested succession route, and ISS finds Cameroonians now hold senior posts in Boko Haram. [11][12]
context_md: Paul Biya has been president since 6 November 1982, when he succeeded Ahmadou Ahidjo. [13] Parliament removed presidential term limits in April 2008, and Freedom House rates the country Not Free. [11] The Anglophone crisis began in October 2016 as protests by teachers and lawyers in the North-West and South-West and became an armed separatist conflict. [10][14] Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) operate in the Far North, where the region became the main hotspot of the Lake Chad Basin in 2025. [12] The October 2025 presidential election, held on the 12th, was followed by protests, mass arrests and the death in custody of the opposition leader Anicet Ekane. [2][15] A constitutional amendment of 14 April 2026 brought back the post of vice president, abolished in 1972. [16][3]

sections.title: A disputed eighth term: 53.66 percent, at least 48 dead and a runner-up in exile
sections.body_md:
The Constitutional Council declared Paul Biya the winner of the 12 October 2025 election on 27 October, with 53.66 percent. His results in 2018 and 2011 were 71 percent and 77 percent. [1] Issa Tchiroma Bakary, a former government minister, declared himself the winner on election day and alleges fraud. [2] His own account is that he finished second with more than 1.6 million votes on the official count. [17] Chatham House puts his claimed share at 54.8 percent, drawn from tally sheets compiled by the opposition and civil society. [1][18] Biya was sworn in on 6 November 2025. [2]

The process drew criticism before the vote. Crisis Group noted in August 2025 that the electoral commission had provisionally approved 13 of 83 candidates and excluded Maurice Kamto, and that most senior officials in the electoral bodies are appointed by the president. [19] Christopher Fomunyoh of the National Democratic Institute wrote that results passed through three commissions before the Council used the full 15 days allowed, and that the removal of Kamto damaged credibility. [18]

Tchiroma fled to The Gambia, where its government has hosted him since November 2025. [20] In June 2026 he filed a complaint in the Paris Judicial Court against Biya and 20 other officials over the repression of protesters, relying on universal jurisdiction. Labour minister Gregoire Owona dismissed it as a bid for attention. [7] Cameroon Concord's Bridget Forjindam argues that his movement has since lost momentum and allies, an opinion-leaning reading. [8] In late October 2026 the Minister of Territorial Administration, Paul Atanga Nji, suspended his party, the National Salvation Front (FSNC), for three months, citing calls for insurrection, threats to public order and a leader living abroad. MANIDEM called the measure unjust. [21]

lenses.local: The Guardian Post and Cameroon Concord give Tchiroma and his critics space, and Journal du Cameroun tracks his exile; none of them reports an independent recount. [17][8][20]
lenses.international: Africanews, AFP and Reuters copy carry the Council's result, the party suspension and the new election date. [22][21][4]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House and the Journal of Democracy describe a thin official margin and a Council the opposition sees as aligned with Biya. [1][18]

sections.title: The succession gap: a vice presidency created in April and still empty in November
sections.body_md:
The constitutional amendment of 14 April 2026 reintroduced the vice presidency. The president appoints and dismisses the vice president, and under revised Article 6 that person would finish the term if the presidency fell vacant. If there is no vice president, an election must follow within 20 to 120 days and the Senate president, Aboubakary Abdoulaye, acts as interim head of state. [16][3] As of 10 November no vice president had been publicly named, so the mechanism is untested. [16]

Biya left for Europe on 7 June and returned to Yaounde on 20 August, after about ten weeks in Geneva. Carnegie counts 73 days and Al Jazeera 74. [11][3] During the absence Reuters reported that three decrees replaced commanders in four of five joint military regions and promoted the head of the Presidential Guard to brigadier general. Government spokesman René Emmanuel Sadi told RFI that "the president is alive." [9] Officials denied reports that Biya had been hospitalised in Geneva. [3] Carnegie notes that roughly two-thirds of recent senior military appointees share Biya's Beti ethnic background. [11]

The names in play come from analysts, not from any announcement. Carnegie lists Franck Biya, the president's son, Secretary-General of the Presidency Ferdinand Ngoh Ngoh, former prime minister Philémon Yang, minister Paul Atanga Nji and finance minister Louis-Paul Motazé. [11] On 8 November the ruling party's communications secretary, Jacques Fame Ndongo, said Franck Biya is a citizen who can claim the succession but that nothing is certain. [6] A presidency source quoted by AllAfrica says Biya is aware of clan rivalries and is taking his time. [13] A false decree naming Franck Biya as vice president circulated in April; Africa Check found no such appointment and said the decree lacked the presidency watermark. [23] Biya's promise of a new government "in the coming days" on 31 December 2025 had not been kept by early October. [24]

lenses.local: Journal du Cameroun quotes the ruling party's spokesman on Franck Biya, and opposition leader Cabral Libii told Al Jazeera that the vice presidency is no ordinary post. [6][24]
lenses.international: Reuters and Al Jazeera document the absence, the military decrees and the unfilled post. [9][16]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie rates an empty post at the time of a death as increasingly likely and says it would leave the process in uncharted territory; Chatham House warned in 2025 of an elite power struggle without an accepted successor. [11][1]

sections.title: The crackdown: up to 2,000 detained, an opposition leader dead in custody
sections.body_md:
Human Rights Watch put the death toll from the post-election protests at 48 killed by security forces according to UN sources cited by media, and 55 according to opposition sources. Communication minister Sadi said on 6 November 2025 that "several dozen" had died. [2] A pool of 149 pro-bono lawyers estimated that up to 2,000 people were detained, including minors, and HRW reviewed lists naming 312 detainees, 154 of whom had not seen a judge. Charges include insurrection and hostility against the homeland, and some carry the death penalty. [2] Al Jazeera reported in November 2026 that some detainees remain in custody. [4]

Anicet Ekane, 74, leader of MANIDEM, was arrested in Douala on 24 October 2025 and held at the State Defense Secretariat in Yaounde, where HRW has documented torture. He died on 1 December. His family and lawyers say he was denied medical care and his oxygen concentrator was seized. The government said he died after an illness and the Defence Ministry opened an inquiry. HRW asked for an independent investigation. [15] Tchiroma later dedicated an online broadcast to him. [17]

The wider pattern is of narrowing room. Crisis Group recorded the suspension and banning of civil society groups before the vote, and Atanga Nji's three-month suspension of the FSNC came in October 2026, three months before the legislative polls. [19][21]

lenses.local: Tchiroma's allies and the FSNC are the main local voices on detentions; Journal du Cameroun records the party's denials of disinformation. [17][20]
lenses.international: AFP, Al Jazeera and Africanews report the arrests, the Ekane death and the party suspension. [4][21]
lenses.scholar: HRW is the main source on deaths and detention; its counts rest on lawyers' lists, opposition figures and UN sources cited by media. [2][15]

sections.title: Press freedom: journalists held over a photo, lost glasses and a deportation story
sections.body_md:
CPJ documented three cases in 2026. On 17 February judicial police in Yaounde detained four journalists, among them an Associated Press crew, for about five hours and seized phones and a laptop after they photographed a centre holding deportees secretly flown out of the United States. They were investigated for trespass and not charged. [25] On 10 August soldiers in Buea detained George Atabong Lekeaka after he posted a photo of a patrol during clashes with separatists, and held him incommunicado until CPJ's report on 14 August, after which his lawyer said he was released. [26]

On 14 and 16 September four journalists were arrested on suspicion of stealing economy minister Alamine Ousmane Mey's glasses at a Yaounde conference. The glasses were later found in his car. They spent five to seven nights in police cells and were released on 21 September without charge. Sadi called it an unfortunate incident caused by excessive zeal. The journalists' union announced a boycott of coverage of the minister's events. [27]

Debate on Biya's health has been banned in the media since 2024. [4][11] On World Press Freedom Day Tchiroma accused the government of targeting independent journalism, a political claim that Cameroon Concord reported alongside RSF's concerns about colonial-era media laws. [28]

lenses.local: Mimi Mefo Info, founded in 2018, says it employs about 20 journalists and covers the Anglophone crisis and the Far North; its chief executive calls press freedom a national problem. That interview dates from 2023. [29]
lenses.international: AP's own crew was detained while reporting on third-country deportations, which makes the case a US story as well. [25]
lenses.scholar: CPJ is the main monitor and its alerts rely on lawyers and the journalists themselves. [27][26]

sections.title: Ten years in the Anglophone regions: lower intensity, school lockdowns and contested tolls
sections.body_md:
Crisis Group's April 2026 report, as relayed by Journal du Cameroun, counts more than 6,500 deaths since 2017, while the Canadian refugee board quotes the same source at over 7,000 deaths, about one million displaced and 600,000 pupils out of school at the peak. [30][31] Al Jazeera and AFP cite the UN at at least 6,000 dead since 2016. [10] OHCHR noted in January 2026 reduced intensity but continuing grave abuses by both sides, and OCHA said in February that about 45 percent of schools in the two regions do not function. [31]

The school year again opened under a lockdown. Separatist leaders announced a weeklong lockdown that began on 7 September, and on 8 September armed men infiltrated a teacher training centre in Wum, killed a police officer and took five teachers, according to North-West governor Adolphe Lele Lafrique. [10][32] On 14 September gunmen on motorcycles shot patrons in a Bamenda bar, killing at least three, and police reports cited by Xinhua count at least 10 deaths since the lockdown began. [32] Similar lockdowns hit the first two weeks of the 2024 school year. [33]

Figures are contested. In April the Defence Ministry said it killed 14 alleged separatists at Ndzerem-Nyam, while local sources and civil society said at least 15 civilians were killed. [31] ACLED recorded 39 deaths in 2026 up to late May around plantations and civilians, and 36 incidents around plantations of the state-owned Cameroon Development Corporation, which employs nearly 20,000 people. In 2025 it recorded 80 such incidents. [34] Government says the state is one and indivisible and favours decentralization within the Special Status. [14]

lenses.local: Mimi Mefo Info and Journal du Cameroun cover the regions; this draft read only an older Mimi Mefo Info report on lockdowns and not its 2026 coverage. [33][30]
lenses.international: AFP and Xinhua file on spikes such as the Wum attack and the Bamenda shooting, not on the steady daily toll. [10][32]
lenses.scholar: Chatham House's October 2026 podcast describes a muted international response and limited results from mediation and the national dialogue. [35]

sections.title: The Far North: Cameroonian commanders inside Boko Haram and ISWAP pressure on border posts
sections.body_md:
ISS researcher Célestin Delanga reports that the Far North became the main hotspot in the Lake Chad Basin in 2025. He counts 714 reported Boko Haram attacks in 2025 under Cameroonian commanders and 227 from January to June 2026. At least five Cameroonian commanders lead about 400 fighters each, roughly 1,000 in Mayo-Sava and Mayo-Tsanaga, and they use family ties, border markets and stolen livestock to raise money. [12] He urges a defection programme and says the existing demobilisation scheme lacks incentives. [12]

On 16 September, armed men killed 15 people in Madegoua village near Makary. Hundreds fled toward Kousseri, Mora and Waza, and displaced residents said they received no government help. No group claimed the attack, and a security analyst told Reuters that ISWAP was the likely perpetrator. [36] The date of the attack is inferred from the report's 'Wednesday' and its publication on 22 September. [36]

Africa Defense Forum, citing an ISS study, says ISWAP has attacked 10 military outposts since January 2026, leading to the dismantling of some border posts, and taxes residents of Darak. [37] ACLED recorded in July the highest violence in Mayo-Tsanaga since July 2025 and reported that the United States has started exploring military cooperation in the Far North, including a May meeting between Biya and a US Africa Command deputy commander. [38] Cameroon Tribune, a state-owned daily, attributes the surge partly to recruitment of Cameroonians and weaker cooperation between stakeholders. [39]

lenses.local: The state-owned Cameroon Tribune is the only Cameroonian outlet read for this section, and it is flagged state-affiliated. [39]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and Reuters carry the Madegoua raid and ISWAP attribution. [36]
lenses.scholar: ISS and ACLED supply the counts and the analysis of Cameroonian command roles and US interest. [12][38]

sections.title: Money: a 40 percent debt ratio, a shrinking oil line and a debt wall flagged for 2026 and 2027
sections.body_md:
The IMF's March 2026 Article IV release estimates 2025 growth at 3.1 percent, with 3.3 percent projected for 2026, and public debt at 40.3 percent of GDP in 2025. It still rates the risk of debt distress as high. Oil nominal receipts are projected to fall from CFAF 1,017 billion in 2024 to CFAF 791 billion in 2026 and CFAF 648 billion in 2027. [40] The non-oil primary deficit was 2.6 percent of GDP in 2025 against a budget target of 1.4 percent, and the Board urged an exit from the FATF grey list. [40]

An IMF staff mission in September 2026 reports 2025 growth of 3.5 percent, a slight slowdown in 2026, average inflation of 2.6 percent through August and a 2025 deficit of 2.1 percent of GDP. Cameroon has no IMF programme, and the Board is expected to take up the assessment in December 2026. [41] The two IMF documents differ on 2025 growth. [40][41]

Crisis Group, via Journal du Cameroun, warns of a debt wall in 2026 and 2027 and a liquidity risk. [30] Al Jazeera quotes analysts who say the delay in naming a government hurts investor confidence. [3] ACLED shows that the state-owned plantation company CDC could stop working in the most dangerous areas if violence escalates. [34]

lenses.local: Journal du Cameroun is the only local outlet read here and it reports Crisis Group's warning, not its own analysis. [30]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera links the reshuffle delay to investor confidence. [3]
lenses.scholar: The IMF and Crisis Group supply the debt and liquidity assessments. [40][30]

sections.title: 2.9 million need aid, and last year's plan reached about half the target
sections.body_md:
The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan says about 2.9 million people need assistance and protection, partners target 1.9 million of them, and US$319 million is required. In 2025 about one million people received help out of 2.1 million targeted. Priority regions are the Far North, North-West, South-West, North, Adamawa and East. [5]

WFP's March 2026 brief expects about 2.9 million people in IPC Phase 3 or worse from June to August 2026, including 250,000 in Phase 4. It counts over 2.2 million forcibly displaced people, among them 408,620 refugees, about one million internally displaced people and 790,850 returnees, and puts stunting at 29 percent of children under five. [42] The identical 2.9 million figures come from two different measures, need for aid and food insecurity. [5][42]

The Madegoua raid shows how new displacement follows attacks. Displaced residents near Waza slept in the open and reported no food, according to a local health official. [36] AFP's background on the Anglophone conflict says about 100,000 people have fled to Nigeria. [10]

lenses.international: Al Jazeera and AFP relay displacement figures at moments of violence. [36][10]
lenses.scholar: OCHA and WFP are the main sources; their plans cover Anglophone, Far North and refugee needs together. [5][42]

timeline.text: Biya becomes president after Ahmadou Ahidjo's resignation.
Anglophone protest movement begins in the North-West and South-West.
Crisis Group warns that the October election is a stress test for stability.
Presidential election held; Tchiroma declares himself winner.
Constitutional Council declares Biya the winner with 53.66 percent.
Biya sworn in for an eighth term.
Opposition leader Anicet Ekane dies in custody.
Constitutional amendment reintroduces the vice presidency.
Biya replaces commanders in four of five joint military regions by decree.
Armed men kill a police officer and kidnap five teachers in Wum.
Raid on Madegoua in the Far North kills 15 and displaces residents of 10 villages.
IMF staff finish a post-financing assessment mission; Board consideration expected in December.
Minister of Territorial Administration suspends the FSNC for three months.
Presidential decree sets legislative and local elections for 7 February 2027.

scores.coverage_basis: Wires and global outlets file on Cameroon when something breaks, such as the October 2025 vote, Biya's absence or an attack in the Far North, and Reuters and AFP copy appears a few times a month. [9][4] Specialist output from Crisis Group, ISS, ACLED and Carnegie is steady but small, and local outlets such as Journal du Cameroun and The Guardian Post publish regularly. [12][38][6][7]

severity.basis: ISS counts 227 Boko Haram attacks in Cameroon from January to June 2026, ACLED sees the highest violence in Mayo-Tsanaga since July 2025, and the Anglophone war has passed 6,500 deaths, with OHCHR noting reduced intensity. [12][38][30][31]
About 2.9 million people need aid, 408,620 refugees and about one million internally displaced people are counted, and 250,000 face IPC Phase 4. [5][42]
At least 48 people were killed in post-election protests, up to 2,000 were detained, Ekane died in custody and the main opposition party was suspended. [2][15][21]
Growth is about 3 percent and debt is about 40 percent of GDP, but the IMF rates debt distress risk as high and oil receipts are falling. [40][41]
The succession post is empty, the party suspension and press cases came in 2026 and Far North attacks rose, while Anglophone intensity eased. [16][21][27][12][31]

parts.basis: The United States is exploring military cooperation in the Far North, and Biya met a US Africa Command deputy commander in May. [38]
Oil receipts are projected to fall from CFAF 1,017 billion in 2024 to CFAF 648 billion in 2027, and the IMF flags volatile cocoa and oil prices. [40]
ISWAP and Boko Haram use border zones with Nigeria and Chad, and Carnegie warns a disputed succession could widen separatist and jihadist reach. [11][12]
Cameroon hosts 408,620 refugees and about 100,000 Anglophone Cameroonians have fled to Nigeria. [42][10]
A vice presidency appointed by the president, term limits removed in 2008 and the use of Cameroon for third-country US deportees make it a test of transfer rules. [16][11][25]

summary: Cameroon matters beyond its borders through the Lake Chad jihadist conflict, a 93-year-old president with no named successor and an Anglophone war that has run for ten years, not through trade or great-power rivalry. [11][12][35]
gi.up: A death or incapacity of Biya with no vice president named, a sharp rise in attacks on border posts, or confirmed US military deployment in the Far North.
gi.down: A named vice president accepted by the main factions, a credible inclusive February 2027 vote, or a mediated Anglophone ceasefire.

reporters.bio: Credited with reporting on Reuters' 4 August 2026 story on the military reshuffle and bylined on Al Jazeera's October and November 2026 pieces from Yaounde.
reporters.why: The main English-language wire and broadcast route for Biya's absence and the delayed reshuffle.

reporters.name: Lesley Anne Warner
reporters.role: Visiting scholar, Africa Program, Carnegie Endowment
reporters.bio: Author of the 8 September 2026 Carnegie Q&A on Biya's absence and the succession.
reporters.why: Lays out the constitutional mechanics and the named candidates for the succession.
reporters.label: Carnegie Endowment

reporters.name: Célestin Delanga
reporters.role: Research officer, West Africa, Sahel and Lake Chad Basin, ISS
reporters.bio: Wrote the August 2026 ISS Today analysis of Cameroonian commanders in Boko Haram.
reporters.why: Gives the attack counts and the command structure in the Far North.
reporters.label: ISS Today

reporters.name: Ladd Serwat
reporters.bio: Author of the May 2026 ACLED comment on violence around state plantations and co-author of its July 2026 Africa overview.
reporters.why: Quantifies the Anglophone plantation violence and tracks US interest in the Far North.
reporters.label: ACLED

reporters.name: Christopher Fomunyoh
reporters.role: Senior associate for Africa, National Democratic Institute
reporters.bio: Wrote the November 2025 Journal of Democracy piece on the election.
reporters.why: An insider read of how results were compiled and why the Council's decision lacked credibility.
reporters.label: Journal of Democracy

reporters.name: Ilaria Allegrozzi
reporters.role: Senior Africa researcher, Human Rights Watch
reporters.bio: Quoted in HRW's November and December 2025 releases on the post-election crackdown and Ekane's death.

reporters.label: Human Rights Watch

reporters.name: Mimi Mefo Takambou
reporters.bio: Founded the online outlet in 2018 and, per its 2023 interview, is based in the UK.
reporters.why: Her outlet covers the Anglophone crisis, the Far North and national news and has a French-language arm.
reporters.label: Mimi Mefo Info

reporters.name: Arnaud Nicolas Mawel
reporters.bio: Bylined on the February 2026 report on Tchiroma's stay in The Gambia and the 9 November 2026 interview with the ruling party's spokesman.
reporters.why: Covers opposition and succession politics for a French-language outlet.
reporters.label: Journal du Cameroun

books.why: An account of France's counterinsurgency against Cameroon's independence movement and how it shaped the post-independence state.

books.author: Mufor Atanga
books.why: Traces Anglophone exclusion from the 1961 federation to the 1990s and rejects the claim that integration succeeded.

podcasts.title: 10 years of Cameroon's Anglophone crisis
podcasts.guest: Dr Jacqui Cho and Hubert Kinkoh
podcasts.why: Covers the conflict economy, the splits in the separatist movement and paths to peace.

factchecks.claim: President Biya appointed his son Franck Biya as vice president and head of the armed forces.
factchecks.evidence: Africa Check found no report of an appointment, including from state media, and the circulating decree lacks the presidency watermark. Cameroon News Agency said the post had not yet been created. Al Jazeera reports that in June a separate decree naming a vice president was delivered to the state broadcaster CRTV, the government said it was not issued properly, and the person was detained.

sources.title: Online posts falsely claim Cameroon leader Paul Biya appointed his son as vice president
Cameroonians await government reshuffle after Biya's return

factchecks.claim: Biya died or was hospitalised in Geneva during his 2026 absence.
factchecks.evidence: Biya returned on 20 August and was filmed by supporters, and a government spokesman said he was alive on 2 August. Officials denied the hospitalisation. Questions over his health persist because media debate about it is banned.

sources.title: As President Paul Biya returns to Cameroon, can he still rule?
Cameroon's Biya, unseen for 58 days, reshuffles military leadership

factchecks.claim: Biya won the October 2025 election with 53.66 percent.
factchecks.evidence: The Council declared 53.66 percent for Biya on 27 October 2025. Tchiroma says he won, and Chatham House cites his claimed share as 54.8 percent from tally sheets. No independent recount exists. Crisis Group and NDI's Fomunyoh raised concerns about the electoral bodies.

sources.title: Suppression of post-election protests in Cameroon will not solve the country's looming succession crisis
Cameroon's Election Casts a Long Shadow

gaps: Local sourcing is partial: Mimi Mefo Info's 2026 reporting could not be read (only a 2023 interview and a 2024 lockdown report were opened), and Actu Cameroun and CRTV were not read at all.
The Guardian Post, Cameroon Concord and Journal du Cameroun were read through single articles each, and the Guardian Post's Tchiroma claims about threats and medication are his own statements.
Cameroon Tribune is state-owned and is flagged state-affiliated; Al Jazeera, Xinhua and Africa Defense Forum are also flagged for state funding or ownership.
Crisis Group's April 2026 report was read only through Journal du Cameroun and the Canadian IRB summary, which give different death tolls (over 6,500 and over 7,000).
The two IMF documents differ on 2025 growth (3.1 and 3.5 percent), and the Article IV release is internally inconsistent on inflation.
The 16 September date of the Madegoua attack is inferred from a Wednesday reference in a report published 22 September, and the death toll comes from that single report.
The date of the FSNC suspension is given only as the Tuesday before 29 October; the exact date was not confirmed.
Biya's absence is reported as 73, 74 or about 10 weeks depending on the source.
Deaths in the post-election protests have no official count; 48 and 55 are UN-source and opposition estimates relayed by HRW.
The podcast and documentary links point to listing pages and streaming availability was not checked.
No fact-check was found on claims about the Anglophone death toll.

HRW is the main source on deaths and detention; its counts rest on lawyers' lists, opposition figures and UN sources cited by media. [2][15]

CPJ is the main monitor and its alerts rely on lawyers and the journalists themselves. [27][26]

Chatham House's October 2026 podcast describes a muted international response and limited results from mediation and the national dialogue. [35]

ISS and ACLED supply the counts and the analysis of Cameroonian command roles and US interest. [12][38]

The IMF and Crisis Group supply the debt and liquidity assessments. [40][30]

OCHA and WFP are the main sources; their plans cover Anglophone, Far North and refugee needs together. [5][42]
